extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, supervisory patent examiners, Technology Center staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on when and how to conduct Patentability Reports, perform prior art searches, determine patentability under 35 U.S.C. (101/102/103/112), articulate rejections vs objections, and related procedural requirements during examination and reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Patentability Report (PR) practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability Report practice is not obligatory and should be resorted to only where it will save total examiner time or result in improved quality of action due to specialized knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practice is based on the proposition that when plural, indivisible inventions are claimed, examination or results may be better when specialists treat claims directed to their specialty. However, a single examiner may often give a complete examination in less total examiner time. Use PR only when it saves total examiner time or improves quality; primary importance is saving total examiner time required to give a complete examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: When PR practice is improper — same character claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claims are directed to the same character of invention but differ in scope only, prosecution by Patentability Report is never proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use PR when claims share the same character irrespective of scope differences; PR suits cases of plural, distinct specialties only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary situations where PRs are ordinarily not proper
rubrics_metrics.description: PRs are ordinarily not proper where claims are related as (A) manufacturing process and a product defined by the process, (B) product and a process that merely makes that product, or (C) combination distinguished solely by characteristics of a subcombination and such subcombination per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In situations (A)-(C) the examiner of the product or process usually can make a complete and adequate examination in less total examiner time; do not assign PRs in such cases absent special justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval required for PR where it saves time
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it can be shown that a Patentability Report will save total examiner time, one is permitted with the approval of the Director of the Technology Center to which the application is assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approval must be documented (the 'Approved' stamp on the memorandum requesting the Patentability Report) and obtained before implementing PR practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting and recording Patentability Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The forwarding of the application for a Patentability Report is not to be treated as a transfer by the forwarding Technology Center (TC). When the P.R. is completed and the application is ready for return to the forwarding TC, it is not counted either as a receipt or action by transfer. Credit is given for the time spent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Date status in reporting TC determined on basis of dates in TC of original jurisdiction; timely reminder should be furnished to TC making the P.R. to ensure orderly progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate prints of drawings for PRs
rubrics_metrics.description: In Patentability Report applications having drawings, the examiner assigned will furnish prints of applicable drawing sheets to the TC to which the application is referred for interference search purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate that duplicates were furnished (e.g., pencil notation on file wrapper or IFW processing). When an application with PR prosecution is passed for issue or abandoned, notify each TC that submitted a PR at once; reporting TC examiners should note allowance or abandonment dates on duplicate prints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting TC participation in interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: In situations where an interview is held on an application in which a Patentability Report has been adopted, the reporting Technology Center may be called on for assistance at the interview when it concerns claims treated by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP § 713–713.10 regarding interviews; involve reporting TC when their treated claims are at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination process before rejecting claims
rubrics_metrics.description: After the application has been read and the claimed invention understood, a prior art search for the claimed invention is made; with search results the application should be reviewed and analyzed in conjunction with the state of the prior art to determine whether the claims define a useful, novel, nonobvious, and enabled invention that has been clearly described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goal is to clearly articulate any rejection early in prosecution so applicant can reply; examiner should review all evidence, including applicant arguments and responsive evidence, before issuing the next Office action. If information reasonably necessary should be required under 37 CFR 1.105, do so prior to or with the first Office action on the merits per MPEP § 704.10 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's dual role — reject and allow appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Although procedures for rejecting claims are explained, the examiner should never overlook the importance of his or her role in allowing claims which properly define the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not focus solely on rejections; allow claims when they meet patentability standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for rejection — 37 CFR 1.104(c) (must reject unpatentable claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention is not considered patentable, or not considered patentable as claimed, the claims, or those considered unpatentable will be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rejecting for want of novelty or obviousness, cite the best references available; designate the particular part relied on when a reference is complex; clearly explain the pertinence of each reference if not apparent; specify each rejected claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on admissions and facts known to examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: In rejecting claims the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant, or the patent owner in a reexamination proceeding, as to any matter affecting patentability and, insofar as rejections in applications are concerned, may also rely upon facts within his or her knowledge pursuant to paragraph (d)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions in specification or made during prosecution can support anticipation or obviousness determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subject matter developed by another in 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter developed by another which qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f), or (g) may be used as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103 against a claimed invention unless the entire rights to the subject matter and the claimed invention were commonly owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where common ownership or obligation of assignment exists, 103 rejection based on those 102(e)/(f)/(g) references is inappropriate; see the joint research agreement exception and requirements for applicant statement under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) to overcome such a rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint research agreement exception for 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection based on subject matter qualifying as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f), or (g), the applicant must provide a statement that the prior art and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. Applicant must amend/disclose parties as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory invention registration preclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in any original application naming an inventor will be rejected as being precluded by a waiver in a published statutory invention registration naming that inventor if the same subject matter is claimed in the application and the statutory invention registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar rejection applies in reissue applications under specified conditions. Ensure record shows whether subject matter was waived in the statutory invention registration and whether claims seek the same subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform application of patentability standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The standards of patentability applied in the examination of claims must be the same throughout the Office. All requirements for patentability (novelty, usefulness and unobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, and 103) must be met before a claim is allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 'preponderance of the evidence' test: reject if, in view of prior art and record evidence, it is more likely than not the claim is unpatentable. A 'picture' claim reciting all features is not justification for allowance by itself. Issues pertinent to patentability must be raised and resolved during examination/prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defects in form or omission of a limitation — constructive action
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application discloses patentable subject matter but the claims in their present form cannot be allowed because of defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection or rejection of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner’s action should be constructive and, when possible, offer a definite suggestion for correction rather than mere objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noting patentable subject matter disclosed but not claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner is satisfied that patentable subject matter has been disclosed in the specification but not claimed, the examiner may note in the Office action that certain aspects or features of the patentable invention have not been claimed and that, if properly claimed, such claims may be given favorable consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a way to prompt applicant to amend claims to cover patentable aspects that were disclosed but overlooked in the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration after applicant reply — continued examination (37 CFR 1.112)
rubrics_metrics.description: After reply by applicant to a non-final action, the application will be reconsidered and again examined. Applicant will be notified if claims are rejected, objections made, or decisions favorable to patentability are made in the same manner as after the first examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may reply with or without amendment unless action is final or an appeal/closing action has been taken. Amendments prior to an appeal brief are subject to 37 CFR 1.116(b) and (c). Follow specified procedures and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between rejection and objection
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to grant claims because the subject matter as claimed is considered unpatentable is called a 'rejection.' If the form of the claim (as distinguished from its substance) is improper, an 'objection' is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term 'rejected' for substantive rejections; objections are formal matters reviewable by petition to the Director, not by the Board (the Board will not decide pure formal objections). Do not combine formal matters improperly in appeals to the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art rejections should use the best available art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art rejections should ordinarily be confined strictly to the best available art; merely cumulative rejections that would fall if the primary rejection is not sustained should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Back up rejections with best alternative art where appropriate; exercise caution in selecting references and in combining references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on abstracts and foreign-language documents
rubrics_metrics.description: When an abstract is used to support a rejection, the evidence relied upon is the facts contained in the abstract, not additional facts in the underlying full text document. If both abstract and underlying document qualify as prior art, obtain and analyze a copy of the underlying document and translation (if not English) so the record is clear as to the precise facts the examiner relies upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full text document may fully anticipate or teach away from the invention; record must show whether examiner relies on abstract or full text. In limited circumstances, a non-final Office action may base a rejection on an abstract alone, but the full text and translation should be supplied in the next Office action; whether that next action may be made final is governed by MPEP § 706.07(a). Obtain full texts at earliest practicable time to improve quality and reduce pendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance upon admitted prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement by an applicant in the specification or made during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art' is an admission which can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify under statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitted prior art can be used to reject claims even where it might not meet statutory categories; see MPEP § 2129 for admissions discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) and 103 (obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: For anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102, the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention either explicitly or implicitly (any feature not directly taught must be inherently present). Under 35 U.S.C. 103, reference teachings must be modified in a manner that would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the two distinctions in mind when formulating rejections; see MPEP § 2131–§ 2146 for detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the effective filing date of the application
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective filing date rules: (A) continuation/divisional applications have the earliest filing date if 35 U.S.C. 120/365(c) satisfied; (B) continuation-in-part: claims not supported by parent have effective filing date equal to new application; claims fully supported have parent's filing date; (C) foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119/365: effective filing date is U.S. filing date unless (A) or (B) applies; (D) proper 119(e) provisional benefit gives provisional filing date for claims fully supported by provisional under first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP sections referenced for details on PCT national stage differences; correct effective date determination is critical to choosing which prior art applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections corresponding to claims of a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims corresponding to claims of a patent are presented in an application, the examiner must determine whether the presented claims are unpatentable on any ground(s) (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, 112, double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a ground of rejection would also be applicable to claims in the corresponding patent, any office action including the rejection must have approval of the Technology Center Director; follow MPEP § 1003 and related interference guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the reference's issue or publication date
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must determine the issue or publication date of the reference so proper comparison between application and reference dates can be made. A magazine is effective as a printed publication under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as of the date it reached the addressee and not the date it was placed in the mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 707.05(f) and MPEP § 2124, § 2126, § 2128–§ 2128.02 for case law on reference date determination; accurate dating affects which 102 subsection applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying 35 U.S.C. 102(b) — statutory bar timing
rubrics_metrics.description: If the publication or issue date of the reference is more than 1 year prior to the effective filing date of the application, the reference qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) (statutory bar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: when the last day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or Federal holiday, the effective filing date may be the next succeeding business day (Ex parte Olah). Recent rules on Express Mail filing do not affect applicant's concurrent right to defer filing to the next business day in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying 35 U.S.C. 102(e) — inventive entity and dates
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply a reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the inventive entity of the application must be different than that of the reference; with joint inventors, only one inventor needs to be different for inventive entities to be different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revised 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (AIPA and later amendments) applies in examining all applications and is retroactive to Nov 29, 2000, with limited exceptions for certain international applications filed prior to that date. Determine which version of 102(e) applies by reference filing dates and international application publication conditions (e.g., PCT Article 21(2) in English). See MPEP § 706.02(f)(1) for guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to consider 102(a), (b), or (e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a printed publication or patent that discloses the claimed invention is found, the examiner should determine whether the rejection should be made under 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e) by comparing the effective filing date of the application with the date of the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First consider 102(b) because it results in a statutory bar; if 102(b) does not apply due to timing, consider 102(e) and the inventive entity criteria; follow MPEP guidance on dating and reference qualification.
